item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have turned their eyes to the offseason.
It’s earlier than they would’ve liked, but they were swept out of the AL Wild Card Series by the New York Yankees, and so now they’ve got to think about what the 2027 campaign will look like.
There’s one area where the Red Sox have the potential to be particularly busy in the offseason — whenever it can begin in earnest after a potential lockout — and that’s salary arbitration.
They’ll have a whopping 17 players up for salary arbitration, if they choose to tender them contracts.
One of the biggest names on that list is Wilyer Abreu, and MLB Trade Rumors writer Matt Swartz has projected values for all the Boston arbitration eligible players.
For Abreu, the number comes out to be quite the bargain.
Wilyer Abreu Contract Projection
The MLBTR projection for Abreu’s salary for the 2027 season comes in at $4.6 million.
For a player with the power, glove and throwing arm of Abreu, it certainly seems like a massive bargain.
That doesn’t consider everything that goes into arbitration, though.
Each player that reaches the major leagues via the minor leagues has six years of club control once they reach the majors.
The first three years have a salary based on the collective bargaining agreement, and they’re considered the pre-arbitration years.
Years four through six of a player’s time with a team are the arbitration years. In each of those offseasons, a player is eligible to go to salary arbitration to determine what he’s paid the following season.
The arbitration process features the team submitting a value and the player submitting one, and the independent arbitrator comes to a conclusion on which one wins out.
Teams and players these days often negotiate in advance to avoid actually going to what can be a contentious hearing, but the value they come out with will still end up close to what it would’ve been in arbitration.
All that said, it matters which year a player is in for the sequence — and this is only Abreu’s first arbitration year. Generally, the first arbitration year comes with the lowest salaries, and they rise in each of the two subsequent years, even if the player is viewed as having exactly the same value each season.
So for Abreu, no matter what he did this season, he wasn’t going to end up with a giant arbitration value.
The Red Sox could always look to give him a higher-paying contract extension and buy out some of his eventual free agent years, but for now, Abreu is headed for arbitration.
Other Red Sox in Arbitration
The list of 17 Red Sox heading to salary arbitration is long.
The full list is: Tanner Houck, Johan Oviedo, Adley Rutschman, Jarren Duran, Eli White, Kutter Crawford, Connor Wong, Romy Gonzalez, Triston Casas, Andruw Monasterio, Zack Kelly, Greg Weissert, Wilyer Abreu, Erik Miller, Justin Slaten, Jahmai Jones and Tyron Guerrero.
If a team chooses not to tender a player a contract, they instead go right to free agency.

item.content:encoded:
The worst news for Boston fans isn't that Roman Anthony is hurt. It is that the injury is worse than anyone thought. New scans revealed fresh muscle strains in his wrist alongside old damage. This changes everything for the Red Sox playoff hopes.
Scans Show Worse Damage
Anthony left Game 1 of the Wild Card Series with soreness after a checked swing. He struck out twice before getting pulled in a 9-0 loss. Manager Chad Tracy said the player was sent back to Boston for more imaging. The results were grim. "We sent him back to Boston for extra, additional imaging which actually revealed some new strains to different muscles in his wrist in addition to exasperating the old injuries. It's not great," Tracy told reporters, per ESPN.
This isn't a minor tweak. The 22-year-old missed 101 games earlier this year with a torn ligament in his right ring finger. He only played 55 regular season games before this latest setback. His stats dropped from a .292 average last year to .245 this season. The Red Sox signed him to a massive $130 million extension hoping for a star. Now that deal looks like a gamble on a broken body.
A Brutal Playoff Rule
There is a cruel twist in the rulebook that fans need to know. If a player gets removed from a playoff roster during a series, he cannot play in the next series either. This means Anthony won't just miss Game 2 against the Yankees. He will be ineligible for the entire ALDS if Boston advances. The team replaced Anthony on the roster with Curtis Mead, according to MLB Trade Rumors.
Tracy tried to frame it as a common issue for players coming off long layoffs. "He's obviously coming off that. You'll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something — it's fine, it goes away," Tracy said. But the reality is different today. "Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable," he added, per ESPN. The hope is gone. The pain is real.
The Cost of a Broken Star
The Red Sox are one loss from elimination. They need every bat they can get. Jahmai Jones is set to hit leadoff as the designated hitter. The lineup includes Adley Rutschman, Willson Contreras, and Wilyer Abreu. Sonny Gray will start on the mound against a former team. But the lineup is missing its most promising young hitter.
Anthony was supposed to be the centerpiece of the next decade. His wrist issues have already cost the team almost four months of the regular season. Now they lose him in the playoffs too. The $130 million contract is secure, but the on-field value is gone for now. Boston has to hope Mead or Seigler can step up immediately. The clock is ticking, and the scans say time is not on their side.

item.content:encoded:
Heading into the Wild Card Series, one could make a case that the Red Sox had a chance to beat the Yankees. It would take two or three great starts from Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and/or Ranger Suarez, it would take some timely hitting to put two or three runs on the board per game, and it would take some lockdown relief innings from the back end of the bullpen.
Yet the Red Sox only got decent starts from Tolle and Gray, they set a new franchise record for offensive utility, and their bullpen was a catastrophe.
And the cherry on top was that their manager, who inked a contract extension last week, showed he certainly does not know how to manage in the postseason.
Other than that, did you enjoy the series?
Here's everything we learned from the ever-so-brief two-game sweep in the Wild Card Series, as the 2026 team technically failed to get as far as the 2025 Red Sox.
Red Sox set ugly new franchise record
Red Sox history spans 126 seasons, so it was a bit surprising to see the broadcast note early in Game 2 that Boston was in the midst of rewriting franchise history with the longest scoring drought to start a postseason ever.
Obviously, the Red Sox' offense has been stagnant (or worse) for weeks, but 26 previous trips to the playoffs, you'd figure that they had started off with a scoreless game and a half before.
Alas, nope. This drought was historic. It ended at 14.2 innings, broken by Willson Contreras' solo shot with two outs in the sixth inning.
And while some of it may be explained by the absences of Roman Anthony and Mickey Gasper, there's no excuse for a playoff team to be this helpless at the plate.
Chad Tracy is not a big-game manager right now
There may have been a case for Chad Tracy to pull Payton Tolle for Erik Miller in Game 1. Not really, but there could have been a case made for Miller's sinker being more effective against Ben Rice than Tolle's fastball.
Yet there's simply no way to understand why one night later, Tracy made the exact same move.
With Sonny Gray at just 70 pitches and the Yankees leading 1-0 with two outs in the fifth inning, Tracy went back to Miller, this time with two runners on base and Cody Bellinger at the plate. The left-left matchup was presumably the reason for the call, but Bellinger crushes sliders from lefties. And when Miller threw a slider to Bellinger ... he delivered.
Bellinger singled home a run, and Miller then gave up another hit to Luis Garcia Jr. The Red Sox only got out of the inning because Rice was caught at home after an aggressive send on that second single.
Gray's pitch count of 70 was tied for his second-lowest of the season, and though he had allowed two singles in the fifth, his body of work over the season and over the past 13 years gave him a much better chance of escaping the mini jam than Miller, who had a 2.045 WHIP and 7.36 ERA in the month of September and who gave up a home run and a single while getting just one out the night before.
If Tracy was insistent that Gray had to come out of the game, he had, quite literally, every high-leverage arm available to him. Instead, he went with Erik Miller.
And with that same complement of arms available in the bottom of the sixth inning, Tracy went with Garrett Crochet, who hasn't pitched in a game since April 25. It didn't go well.
Tracy also showed a lack of feel for the moment when he let leadoff hitter Jahmai Jones, who batted .129 with a .432 OPS over the final 13 games of the regular season and who struck out looking twice, to take his third at-bat in the sixth inning, with the Red Sox trailing 2-0.
Given Boston's offensive ineptitude, the bullpen decisions are perhaps all moot. But had this been a close series, or if the Red Sox find themselves in one in the future, Tracy will carry some major doubt regarding his ability to manage those games.
Simply put, Chad Tracy did not do a single thing right in these two high-stakes games.
More Red Sox Coverage
Luis Garcia Jr.'s home run was great hitting, not bad pitching
It took until the fourth inning for the Yankees to get to Sonny Gray, but the solo homer he allowed to Luis Garcia Jr. didn't come on a bad pitch at all.
Leading off the fourth, Garcia was behind in the count 1-2 when Gray tried to bury a sweeper down and in to the lefty. Gray hit his spot with a pitch that was set to hit the bottom of the strike zone. But Garcia simply stayed on the pitch and went down and got it.
Luis Gar-SEE-YA 🦁 pic.twitter.com/GqxScAqskG
— New York Yankees (@Yankees) October 1, 2026
With the Red Sox starved for runs, Garcia's solo shot was a jarring reminder that all it takes is one good swing to put a run on the board.
Boston eventually got that swing from Contreras in the sixth, but that jolt of hope for the visiting team didn't last long.
What could have been with Garrett Crochet ...
If you just looked at the box score, you'd be shocked to see Garrett Crochet's line. He faced four batters, allowing all of them to score. He didn't record an out, despite getting Spencer Jones to chase strike three to start the sixth inning.
Of course, some of that outcome was fair, as Crochet allowed back-to-back singles. But Caleb Durbin couldn't get the out at first on what was intended to be a sacrifice bunt, Crochet left with the bases loaded, and Garrett Whitlock -- who had a dreadful night -- couldn't limit the damage at all.
Such an outcome was perhaps expected, considering Crochet has not pitched in a game since April 25 due to shoulder problems. But you also can't help but wonder what would have happened if Adley Rutschman and Willson Contreras hadn't combined to bungle Crochet's inning-opening strikeout of Jones.
Rutschman took an extra beat to pounce on the ball that had bounced off his chest, and then he took an extra step before firing to first base. There, Contreras was planted on the back side of the base instead of the front. As a result, Jones was able to beat the throw.
Credit to Aaron Boone for challenging that call, which was initially an out on the field, but really, it wasn't even close.
Rutschman then compounded the matter by sailing a throw into center field when Jones stole second, allowing the runner to take third before scoring on a single. Had Rutschman made either of those two throws, it's fair to wonder how differently Crochet's inning could have gone.
Summing up the season
There will be plenty of time in the coming months to eulogize this season, but really, despite the 32-5 stretch in the summer, it wasn't one to celebrate.
Last year's team won a game in the Wild Card Series, a disappointing ending. This year's team couldn't even do that.
Injuries to Crochet and Anthony were certainly impactful, but this roster -- and particularly the offense -- was not built to contend for a World Series. The Red Sox scored two or fewer runs in 13 of their final 23 games, averaging 2.5 runs per game over that stretch.
With the season on the line, the Red Sox had Jahmai Jones, Nate Eaton and Nick Sogard in their starting lineup.
After trading three of their top-five prospects to acquire Adley Rutschman, the catcher batted .222 with a .688 OPS in the regular season before going 1-for-8 in the playoffs.
Willson Contreras, a 34-year-old former catcher with a lot of MLB miles on him, was worn down by the end of the season. Caleb Durbin, whose lows outnumbered his highs this year, went 0-for-7 in the playoffs. Ceddanne Rafaela posted the same numbers, too.
The return for Marcelo Mayer was Erik Miller, who made a strong first impression but played a pivotal role in sinking the team's chances in both postseason losses after an extremely unreliable final month of the season.
The starting pitching staff was excellent, and the bullpen was elite. But the overall roster construction will lead to plenty of questions about Craig Breslow's ability to build a real winner. Likewise, the two playoff games cast some serious doubt on whether Chad Tracy is a manager capable of winning games in October.
The 15-game winning streak and 32-5 stretch might have led to some internal victory laps and the decisions to stick with Breslow and Tracy for the foreseeable future. But the 2026 Red Sox, on the whole, were what they were: mediocre. And having been stuck in mediocrity (or worse) for half a decade, there won't be much more patience in and around Boston for it to continue.
Technically, the historic season turnaround may have been a positive, as making the playoffs beats bottoming out more often than not. But considering that the Red Sox likely could have loaded up on promising players by selling off veteran pieces like Contreras, Gray, Aroldis Chapman and anyone else at the deadline, that run in July may have hurt the Red Sox in the long term -- especially with the prospect haul that went out to acquire Rutschman.
In any event, the Red Sox finished as the third-best team in the AL East, and they failed to win a single playoff game, getting outscored 18-2 in their lone playoff series. That's the final word on the season as the long offseason -- potentially longer than most -- awaits.

item.content:encoded:
Red Sox's Roman Anthony diagnosed with right hand strain, ineligible to return until ALCS
The Red Sox announced that Roman Anthony would not be in the Boston Red Sox lineup for Game 2 of their AL Wild Card Series against the New York Yankees on Wednesday night, a day after leaving the opener because of hand pain.
In a statement on Wednesday, the team announced that Anthony was diagnosed with a right-hand strain and was substituted off the roster.
Anthony can no longer participate in the remainder of the Wild Card Series or the American League Division Series if Boston advances.
He would be eligible to return for the American League Championship Series.
"I feel sick to my stomach. I haven't slept much. It doesn't feel real, to be honest," Anthony said Wednesday. "I been through so many emotions and feelings to get the same news again and even worse, it's hard to have an answer to anything right now."
The team announced that infielder Curtis Mead will replace Anthony on the Wild Card Series roster.
Anthony said he wasn't sure what the treatment plan would be currently to remedy his hand injury.
"Once we decided I wasn't going to play today, that's all that really mattered," Anthony said. "All that mattered was putting the team in the best situation to win."
Batting leadoff as a designated hitter in his playoff debut Tuesday, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against Cam Schlittler before getting lifted for a pinch hitter with his team trailing by two runs in the sixth inning of a 9-0 loss.
Boston manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings. The 22-year-old Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29 with an injury to the same hand.
"Unfortunately, I checked swing on my second at-bat and I knew right then and there it was time to get it looked and put somebody else in the game that would have a better chance to win," Anthony said.
“He’s obviously coming off that. You’ll get a zinger every once in a while where you feel something — it’s fine, it goes away,” Tracy said. “Today some stuff happened that was more serious and was uncomfortable.”
Jahmai Jones was set to hit leadoff as the DH with the Red Sox one loss from elimination, followed in the batting order by catcher Adley Rutschman, first baseman Willson Contreras, right fielder Wilyer Abreu, center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela, third baseman Caleb Durbin, second baseman Nick Sogard, shortstop Trevor Story and left fielder Nate Eaton.
Sonny Gray was set to start on the mound for Boston against one of his former teams.
One of baseball’s premier prospects when he debuted last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBIs and a .735 OPS in 55 games this season.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Roman Anthony is out for the foreseeable future and is no longer on the Wild Card roster after he left with a right hand injury Tuesday night.
Batting leadoff as the Red Sox designated hitter in his playoff debut, Anthony struck out in both of his at-bats against before getting lifted for a pinch hitter with his team trailing 2-0 in the sixth inning. New York took a 1-0 lead in the best-of-three series with a 9-0 victory.
Manager Chad Tracy said Anthony felt discomfort in his right hand after a couple of checked swings. The 22-year-old Anthony missed 101 games from May 5 to Aug. 29 with an injury to the same hand. Tracy said it doesn't appear the latest injury is necessarily related, as it involves muscles in the wrist.
"After I came back, the hand was never really fully 100%, kind of as you would expect," Anthony told reporters on Wednesday. "Last night just felt a little more intense, little bit more harsh than past swings have and lingered a little bit longer than the ones I was used to had. So it just was super alarming and got to the point where it was tough to grip a bat."
The manager said that after the game, Anthony returned to Boston for imaging on his hand, which found "additional damage to some muscles in his wrist that weren't there before."
Anthony is not in Wednesday night's lineup, when the Red Sox must win to extend their season. Jahmai Jones is leading off at DH in Anthony's absence.
Wednesday night, the team announced that infielder Curtis Mead replaced Anthony on the Wild Card roster. That means that if the Red Sox advance to the ALDS, Anthony would be out for that round as well.
One of baseball's premier prospects when he arrived in the majors last year, Anthony batted .245 with five home runs, 15 RBIs and a .735 OPS in 55 regular-season games this season.
"He's a really good player. Certainly not something we wanted to happen and having him in there is important. But can't reiterate enough, we've dealt with things like this all year. But the show goes on, you've got to play tonight and be able to win a ballgame," Tracy said.
The manager added that it is not yet known if Anthony will need surgery.
Sonny Gray is on the mound for the Red Sox in Game 2, which is scheduled to start at 8:15 p.m.

item.content:encoded:
Lost amid the embarrassing madness of Tuesday's Wild Card series opener between the Boston Red Sox and the New York Yankees was Roman Anthony being pinch-hit for midway through the game, seemingly out of nowhere. After the game, it was revealed by manager Chad Tracy that Anthony had re-aggravated the wrist injury that had kept him out for more than three months during the regular season — and that his Game 2 status was up in the air.
Well, Boston's Game 2 lineup is out, and it's safe to say the fan base won't like it, with Anthony on the bench.
Is Roman Anthony playing tonight? Red Sox's lineup gives answer
Here's a look at Boston's Anthony-less lineup against Yankees left-hander Max Fried.
| Player | Position |
|---|---|
| 1. Jahmai Jones | DH |
| 2. Adley Rutschman | C |
| 3. Willson Contreras | 1B |
| 4. Wilyer Abreu | RF |
| 5. Ceddanne Rafaela | CF |
| 6. Caleb Durbin | 3B |
| 7. Nick Sogard | 2B |
| 8. Trevor Story | SS |
| 9. Nate Eaton | LF |
Yeah, the Red Sox are going to miss Anthony dearly. Sure, there's the makings of a decent lineup here. Jahmai Jones has done nothing but crush lefties since the Red Sox acquired him. Adley Rutschman and Willson Contreras are proven stars. Wilyer Abreu has broken out against left-handers this season, in particular. Ceddanne Rafaela is having his best offensive year. Still, there's no replacing Anthony.
He only appeared in 55 regular-season games and didn't look great in his two at-bats on Tuesday, but nobody in Boston's organization has a higher ceiling than Anthony. Being without him makes the already daunting challenge of rebounding from an 0-1 deficit in the best-of-three series that much more difficult.
Red Sox's growing injury report makes it tougher to believe in dream run
What makes Anthony's injury that much more difficult is that he's far from the only one. The Red Sox have a slew of notables on the IL, and that's making achieving their ultimate gol tough to believe in.
| Player | Position | Injury | Return |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mickey Gasper | C/INF | Right biceps strain | 2027 |
| Tyron Guerrero | RHP | Right shoulder strain | 2027 |
| Eli White | INF/OF | Ligament damage in right foot | 2027 |
| Curtis Mead | INF | Left wrist fracture | Postseason or 2027 |
| Kutter Crawford | RHP | Right flexor irritation | 2027 |
| Johan Oviedo | RHP | Right flexor strain | Postseason or 2027 |
| Anthony Siegler | INF | Right wrist discomfort | Postseason or 2027 |
| Justin Slaten | RHP | Right elbow inflammation | 2027 |
| Masataka Yoshida | DH | Left hamstring strain | Postseason or 2027 |
| Triston Casas | 1B | Left abdominal strain | 2027 |
The list is lengthy and littered with quality talent. Lineup-wise, the Red Sox sure could use Mickey Gasper, who was one of their hottest hitters before suffering his injury, right about now. They could also use Curtis Mead, a player who crushes left-handed pitching. Even Masataka Yoshida's bat would really come in handy with Anthony out.
Pitching-wise, Boston's depth has taken a hit. Tyron Guerrero and Justin Slaten are two of the most important members of their bullpen, and perhaps they would've been able to keep the game closer on Tuesday had they been healthy. Guys like Kutter Crawford and Johan Oviedo are proven back-end starters who could've eaten innings this October.
Perhaps the Red Sox can get Mead and a few others back if they can get past the Yankees, but with Anthony now joining the laundry list of injured players, it's getting tough to believe in them making a comeback.

The Red Sox are in danger of watching their season come to a close in Yankee Stadium for the second consecutive year. The offense showed zero signs of life as the Yankees cruised to a 9-0 victory headlined by 10 strikeouts from growing Red Sox killer Cam Schlittler. Payton Tolle did enough on the mound as the Game 1 starter. His team was clearly just unable to do their part around them.
Now, the Red Sox fall into the need of a historic response given that just 3 of 24 teams to lose the opener in the Wild Card round have come back to win the series. For starters, Boston sends 18-game winner Sonny Gray to the mound. He flirted with a no-hitter the last time he faced New York in June and tallied a 1.98 ERA against the Yankees in 2026.
The Yankees counter with Max Fried, who has battled some inconsistencies in his ramp-up period from an injury return. The southpaw does have a sparkling 1.93 career ERA against the Red Sox in addition to a brilliant start in Game 1 last year with 6 1/3 scoreless innings, which his bullpen ruined in Boston's 3-1 victory. To best combat the talented lefty, Jahmai Jones slots in leading off as the designated hitter. Caleb Durbin moves up to the sixth spot and Nate Eaton – another right-handed bat – gets the nod in left field.
After being shut out in consecutive postseason games, the Red Sox must find a way to score runs and now do so without Roman Anthony, who will come off the ALWC roster with new and aggravated injuries in his right hand. It's an uphill challenge undoubtedly, though it's one Boston must be ready for in order to extend the season.

Get traded away from the Tigers, put up career numbers. It’s a tale as old as time and it’s happening in real time throughout MLB as the playoffs begin.
There are several former Tigers whose new teams have made the playoffs but the headliners have to be Casey Mize and Tarik Skubal. Both joined teams destined for the playoffs at the trade deadline (though Mize was left off the Padres' Wild Card roster). Then there were guys like Jahmai Jones and Jake Rogers who joined hopeful playoff teams — and it ended up working out for them.
The biggest surprise of that group of four former Tigers is probably the fact that Jones has been raking with the Red Sox and may have had the best final two months of the season of the four.
Everyone knew Skubal would be just fine and after posting a 3.00 ERA in August with the Dodgers, he notched a 2.25 ERA in September. He may have gotten hit around a little more than he’s used to with his WHIP creeping over 1.00 with Los Angeles. He was still one of the best pitchers in baseball, but he struggled to adjust at times.
Mize, too struggled with the Padres, posting a 7.46 ERA and 1.68 WHIP after enjoying a 2.70 ERA with the Tigers through the first three months of the season. He also only had 25 strikeouts in 44 innings.
But Jones now looks like the steal of the year, and that's a double-edged sword for the Tigers. They absolutely needed to dump him after his horrendous start to the season, but now he’s hitting the cover off the ball like he did with Detroit in 2025.
Oh, and he’ll be fighting for a World Series berth.
It’s good to see the former Tiger play so well with the Red Sox after struggling through 57 appearances this season and needing a change of scenery. Funny how that always seems to work out, right?
Jahmai Jones has been a revelation with the Red Sox
The Red Sox were already likely to make the playoffs when they acquired Jones and they went 21-16 in games that he played. He was an overall plus player for Boston, posting a 0.8 WAR as well.
What really stands out is his .993 OPS. All he did when he got to Boston was get on base. His on-base percentage is .408 with the Red Sox and he also hit .308 (20-for-65). This is bittersweet to see because the Red Sox are experiencing the same Jones that Tigers fans fell in love with during the 2025 playoff run when he hit .287 with a .937 OPS over 72 games.
Plus, his start to the 2026 season was so bad, there’s no way that anyone in the Tigers’ front office saw him breaking out of a slump like he did with the Red Sox. He hit .137 and had a .440 OPS in 57 games with the Tigers — Detroit was 20-36 in games when he recorded an at-bat.
After getting picked up by the Red Sox in mid-July, Jones got red-hot. His OPS in July was 1.278 which is a video game number and then he doubled down in August with a 1.284 OPS and .474 average. He did come back down to earth in September with a .614 OPS and .182 average over 33 at-bats, but he heads to the postseason with a fresh start again. And we know how that works out for him.
It’s great to see the former Tiger having success with a change of scenery, but it had to come at the expense of a playoff berth for Detroit. The baseball gods have a twisted sense of humor.

Chad Tracy is hardly the only person that has been added to the fold between the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees’ back-to-back meetings in the American League Wild Card Series.
The Red Sox have made substantial additions to the rotation, with Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez being named the starting pitchers for the best-of-three series at Yankee Stadium — making for a much deeper unit than the one that fell off a cliff after Garrett Crochet last season and relied on the likes of Brayan Bello and Connelly Early. Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman, and Caleb Durbin will join the lineup in hopes to scrape together more than the six total runs they scored last season. Crochet could end up joining the bullpen in his return from injury, along with newcomers Erik Miller and Jake Bennett, which is a pretty decent group of pitchers being added to one of the very best units in baseball this season.
The Yankees will also be in a better position on the pitching side, with Gerrit Cole serving as the do-or-die option behind Cam Schlittler and Max Fried. Luis Garcia Jr., Heliot Ramos, and George Lombard Jr. should help the lineup against left-handers, though there is something to be said about the so-so status of Aaron Judge.
If we can boil all of that down, though, only one man can completely swing the series…
Chad Tracy.
Tracy’s most difficult decisions might come before the season even starts, as he will be relied upon heavily to figure out who will fill out the roster — Braiden Ward? Jarren Duran? Curtis Mead? Jahmai Jones? Nate Eaton? Isiah Kiner-Falefa? Crochet?
It’s not going to be easy, but all of that pales in comparison to making decisions with who will play, when they will play, and how he manages things when the lights are at their brightest in The Bronx.
“It’s the playoffs, so we’re at the point in the season where teams that are remaining need to win or they’re going home,” Tracy said during his media availability on Monday. “I have a feel for that.
“… It’s all hands on deck. I think everyone is aware that during the playoffs it’s about winning moments and being aggressive — all those things. I think most of our guys who have been around understand that, so we’re going to go out and play our butts off and manage and do everything we can to win each game.”
Alex Cora, the manager of last year’s squad that became the first in history to lose the best-of-three series after taking a lead, made some… interesting decisions in hindsight.
Bello was pulled after 2 1/3 innings in Game 2, which led to Justin Wilson, Zack Kelly, Garrett Whitlock, and Tolle being used out of the bullpen and becoming unavailable for Game 3. Nate Eaton started over Wilyer Abreu in Game 2. Rob Refsnyder got two starts over Masataka Yoshida, which makes sense considering they faced two left-handers, but he finished 0-for-5 while the latter went 4-for-7. Nathaniel Lowe played in all three games, while Nick Sogard only played in two.
It’s easy to go back in time and poke holes though these decisions with the benefit of hindsight, but that’s kind of the whole point in looking ahead at the same two teams playing each other again with one of them being led by someone new.
Tracy needs to avoid making similar mistakes, and he needs to do it without the benefit of years of experience in similar situations. The Red Sox stripped him of that interim tag because they believe he can, and it’s only a matter of time before we find out whether or not they’re right.

ST. PETERSBURG — After missing eight games, Willson Contreras returned to the Red Sox’s lineup, batting third and serving as designated hitter in Boston’s 6-2 loss to the Cubs in Sunday’s regular-season finale at Tropicana Field.
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy indicated that Contreras, who was hit on the right hand by a pitch on Sept. 17 at Texas, will be active for the American League Wild Card Series, which begins Tuesday night at Yankee Stadium.
“He should be [good to go],’’ Tracy said.
Game 162 was moved from Boston’s Fenway Park to the Trop, home of the Tampa Bay Rays, as a precaution when a weekend nor’easter battered the East Coast with torrential rain and heavy winds. Contreras went 0-for-2 with a strikeout and a groundout before being lifted for pinch-hitter Jahmai Jones in the fifth.
The return of Contreras, who was batting .276 with 27 home runs and 81 RBIs before his injury, was greeted enthusiastically by Tracy and his Red Sox teammates.
“Huge … massive," Tracy said of Contreras’ potential postseason availability. “Even with a layoff, with a guy like that, you know what he’s capable of doing with one swing of the bat. It’s pretty well documented. That’s so much what the postseason is about, these big moments where one swing can change a game. So that power and that presence in the middle of the order is important."
Tracy said Contreras made “pretty significant" improvement and looked impressive in batting practice Saturday, when the Red Sox conducted an optional workout at the Trop during an off-day.
“That was a huge step," Tracy said. “So we’ll get him some live at-bats in a game, and hopefully we’re good to go."
Third baseman Caleb Durbin said Contreras’ return provided energy in the Red Sox clubhouse.
“We’ve been without Willson and Rafa [Ceddanne Rafaela, who missed 17 games with a right quad strain] for a while," Durbin said. “We know what having those guys in the postseason could mean. We’re a different team [with them].
“I think we all feed off [Contreras’] energy. Just having him around and activated is big for us. He’s a big leader. Having that type of experience and energy, with him laying it on the line every single time he’s out there, it will add a lot to the playoff environment. We’re excited to have them back for this level of meaningful baseball."
Along with Contreras’ return, the Red Sox lost a couple of key performers to the injured list. Catcher/first baseman Mickey Gasper was placed on the 10-day IL with a right biceps strain, while right-handed reliever Tyron Guerrero was placed on the 15-day IL with a right shoulder strain.
Gasper batted .251 with 10 homers, 24 RBIs and an .823 OPS in 67 games. Guerrero (a 3.10 ERA in 40 appearances) already had missed most of September because of shoulder inflammation.
The Red Sox recalled infielder/outfielder Nate Eaton and right-handed pitcher Wyatt Olds. Tracy said the organization is still debating how to structure Boston’s postseason roster, but he added that Eaton brings value as an extra outfielder because of his speed and defense.
Another option could be ace left-hander Garrett Crochet, who hasn’t pitched for the Red Sox since April 25 but could return as a reliever. Tracy said Crochet did well during Saturday’s live batting practice session in Fort Myers, Fla. Crochet will likely join Boston in New York, but it’s not yet certain he will be on the postseason roster.

Throughout the season, first baseman Willson Contreras has been the emotional heart for the Boston Red Sox. However, he largely hasn’t been able to play in the month of September due to injuries.
He spent time on the IL due to a hamstring injury. That had been bugging him for some time, and the Red Sox wanted him to reset and get healthy for the postseason. He did, but almost as soon as he came back, he was hit in the right hand by a pitch. That forced Contreras to miss about a week and a half before DHing in the final game of the season on Sunday.
Boston Red Sox Manager Chad Tracy on Willson Contreras in the Playoffs
In the end, Willson Contreras had just two at-bats on Sunday. He’d go 0-2 with a strikeout before Jahmai Jones came in to pinch-hit for him.
It was a small sample size, but it was another emotional boost that Contreras could provide the Red Sox. The postseason is here and he’s healthy enough to play. Better than that, after the game, Red Sox manager Chad Tracy confirmed that he should be available for the Wild Card Round in the postseason.
“He was okay,” Tracy said. “Took the first one [at-bat]. Took the second one. Had a pretty good at-bat. Hit the ball hard to third and he was good. So, I got him out of there… Should be [good to go].
Getting hit on the hand is risky, with plenty of smaller bones to break. Luckily, X-Rays showed that Contreras avoided that, and was just dealing with bad swelling that made it hard to swing a bat. He had previously been anxious about his availability for the postseason when describing it as a bone bruise.
“Yeah, there’s no fracture or anything,” Contreras said. “I had a CT scan yesterday just to make sure that I don’t have any fracture, and it didn’t show any fracture. At this point, still inflammation and a bone bruise.”
This comes at a time when the Red Sox have been desperately trying to get healthy. Players like Adley Rutschman and Caleb Durbin are banged up but playing through it. Others, like Ceddanne Rafaela and Curtis Mead, have needed to spend time on the IL.
Now, the Red Sox will turn their attention ahead to the New York Yankees. The American League Wild Card Series will begin on Tuesday, September 29th in the Bronx. First pitch is scheduled for 8:00 p.m. EST.
It’s Been a Career Season for Contreras
The frustrating part of the injuries for Contreras, other than that it could cost him time in the postseason, is that this has been a career season for him. This comes in his first year with the Red Sox as he’s brought a swing made for Fenway Park to Boston.
He’s hitting .276 with a .905 OPS. Contreras also has 27 home runs and 81 RBIs. That’s in a 129 game effort, and amounted to 4.5 WAR, per Baseball Reference.
Statistically, it’s Contreras’ best season. His previous high for WAR was 4.2 back in 2021. Otherwise, he hadn’t cracked that 4.0 WAR mark before. That was also a new single-season high for home runs and RBIs in his career. So, maybe it shouldn’t be a surprise that’s a career-record for OPS in a season, too.
The Red Sox need that version of Contreras in the postseason. Without him, they’re going to be looking far and wide for their power in the lineup.

item.content:encoded:
Wilyer Abreu has been one of Boston’s most impactful all-around players, but lately the talented right fielder has been stuck in a serious rut.
Over the past few weeks Abreu has seen his offensive production fall off a cliff. Coming into the day he was batting .177 with a .546 OPS and four extra-base hits over his last 17 games since Sept. 3, and during Friday’s doubleheader he started 0 for 7 his first seven trips to the plate.
That kind of slump will put a strain on anyone’s confidence, but after striking out in the bottom of the sixth, Abreu said he was approached by veteran teammate Sonny Gray, who gave him a badly needed pep talk.
“It helped me a lot,” Abreu said. “He’s a vet, he’s got a lot of years here and how to handle those situations, so he give me good advice to feel good with my body, with my athleticism, and trust myself, try to get my confidence back and that was huge.”
The next time up, Abreu reminded everyone at Fenway Park who he really is.
Abreu’s go-ahead two-run double in the bottom of the eighth was the difference in Friday night’s 2-0 win over the Chicago Cubs. The right fielder stepped to the plate with two on and two outs in a scoreless game and crushed an opposite-field line drive high off the Green Monster.
That swing helped the Red Sox seal the doubleheader sweep, and the two clubs will now fly to St. Petersburg to get out ahead of the impending nor’easter to finish the regular season on Sunday at Tropicana Field.
In what was likely his final appearance of the regular season, Brayan Bello capped off his season of turbulence and redemption in style. The right-hander threw four-plus scoreless innings, held the Cubs to four hits and a walk and struck out two while throwing 39 of his 58 pitches for strikes.
Bello wraps up the year with a 4.33 ERA, a deceptively average mark for what was an extraordinarily unique journey. After earning himself a demotion following a disastrous first half that saw him lose his spot in the rotation, Bello finished the season with a 2.11 ERA over 55 1/3 innings in his last 14 appearances since being called back up just prior to the All-Star break.
Following the game Bello said he’s happy and grateful for the way his season ended, adding that the whole year was a big learning experience.
“I learned not to let bad moments dictate how the next one is going to be,” Bello said via interpreter Carlos Villoria Benítez. “Also I learned how to compete in the zone, I feel like in the second half I was able to compete in the zone and beat hitters in the zone, something that I wasn’t able to do in the first half.”
Bello gave way to rookie Jedixson Paez, who was called up between the two games and who has also endured an eventful first year in the majors. The 22-year-old had never pitched above Single-A prior to this season before he was poached by the Chicago White Sox in the Rule 5 Draft, and the right-hander made three uninspiring appearances for the White Sox before he was returned to Boston.
After spending most of the season in the Red Sox minor league system, he was called back up for a spot start on Sept. 1 and got shelled, allowing eight runs in 3 2/3 innings in a loss to the Seattle Mariners. But needing to cover some innings ahead of the club’s upcoming playoff run, Paez came through and gave the Red Sox five scoreless frames in what was by far the best outing of his MLB career so far.
“The first chance he got it didn’t probably go how he wanted and he gets another opportunity and goes out there and spins five scoreless innings and attacks the zone,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “It was awesome.”
Offensively the Red Sox were stymied by Cubs starter David Peterson, who held Boston to three hits and two walks over five shutout innings. The Red Sox had runners reach third base in both the third and fourth innings but couldn’t get the go-ahead runner home.
Boston didn’t fare much better against the Cubs bullpen, but the Red Sox finally got another chance in the bottom of the eighth when Isiah Kiner-Falefa and Jahmai Jones each walked to put two men on with two outs.
That brought Abreu to the plate to face left-hander Ryan Rolison, and the outfielder smoked an opposite-field line drive 100.5 mph off the bat high off the Green Monster. Kiner-Falefa and Jones both came around to score, and that was all she wrote.
Paez returned for the top of the ninth despite initially seeming to deal with a cramping issue while warming up, but after a brief visit by the trainer, he stayed in the game and sent the Cubs down 1-2-3 to end the game.
With this weekend’s finale relocated to St. Petersburg, Fla., Friday night marked the final regular season game at Fenway Park this season. The next time the Red Sox are back in Boston, it will either be for Game 3 of the American League Divisional Series against the Tampa Bay Rays, or for the end-of-the-season press conference should the club lose to the Yankees in the Wild Card round again.
Before they even knew when and where their last game would be, Tracy told his players to prepare to spend 11 days on the road, and Abreu said the team is determined to bring playoff baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021.
“I think the fans deserve it,” Abreu said. “It’s been five years that Boston hasn’t seen any playoff games, so I think we have to give them that opportunity to see playoff games again here at Fenway Park.”
In the meantime, the Red Sox and Cubs will play one more at Tropicana Field on Sunday starting at 3:05 p.m.

Wilyer Abreu broke a scoreless deadlock with a two-out, two-run double in the eighth inning, lifting the Boston Red Sox to a 2-0 win and a doubleheader sweep over the visiting Chicago Cubs on Friday evening.
Abreu was in a 0-for-11 slump before smacking the big hit high off the Green Monster in left-center field. Isiah Kiner-Falefa and Jahmai Jones both walked to set the stage for Abreu’s heroics, with the first walk coming off Chicago’s initial reliever Javier Assad (6-2) in an eventual loss.
The Red Sox (87-74) were limited to just four hits, but Jedixson Paez (1-1) made them stand up while dealing the final five innings en route to his first big-league win. Paez, who was recalled from Triple-A Worcester in between games, scattered three hits, struck out five and did not issue a walk in relief of starter Brayan Bello.
The Cubs (88-73) had seven hits, including two apiece by Seiya Suzuki, Michael Busch and Nico Hoerner.
After Chicago starter David Peterson fanned six across five innings of three-hit ball, Assad had struck out the heart of the Boston lineup in order in the sixth and retired the first six men he faced.
Bello escaped a near-immediate jam in the first. After striking out leadoff hitter Pete Crow-Armstrong, Suzuki walked and Busch dunked a single into shallow left field, but back-to-back outs in the air ended the threat.
The Boston righty also induced double plays to halt potential rallies after leadoff singles by Hoerner in the second and Busch in the fourth. Kiner-Falefa made a diving stop and spun a 4-6-3 ball to erase Hoerner.
Paez replaced Bello following Hoerner’s leadoff knock in the fifth. Matt Shaw lined a two-out single that ricocheted off the umpire standing up the middle before runners were stranded on the corners.
Meanwhile, the Red Sox were hitless until Kiner-Falefa opened the third with a line-drive single to center. He reached third on Anthony’s knock to right, but Peterson retired the next two.
In the fifth, a leadoff walk to Kiner-Falefa was wasted.
The teams’ season finale was moved to Sunday at a neutral location in St. Petersburg, Fla., due to inclement weather expected to impact Boston all weekend.
–Field Level Media

The Red Sox begin the postseason on Tuesday and have scored just 5 runs over the last 5 games. In other words, now would be a great time for the team's best offensive contributor to return to a lineup that desperately needs a spark. But unless a miracle happens over the weekend, things aren't looking good. Willson Contreras took batting practice on Tuesday, only for his hand injury to worsen in the subsequent days. He's still struggling to grip a bat and admitted to tearing up out of frustration. "I'm doing everything that I can to come back and play with the boys and be there with the boys," he said. "But sometimes you have to listen to your body." (Tim Healey, Boston Globe)
At least Ceddanne Rafaela has returned. He should be able to give a little lift for the lineup, though he does present a conundrum for Chad Tracy, as the Sox now have too many outfielders and DHs to fit into the lineup at once. With Roman Anthony, Rafalea, and Wilyer Abreu essentially locked into starting spots, Tracy has to decide whether to prioritize Duran's glove and legs over the platoon DH production of Mickey Gasper and Jahmai Jones. (Sean McAdam, MassLive)
And all of this is occuring against the backdrop of this weekend's storm. And if you think we're done dealing with that now that MLB has moved Sunday's game to today, we're not. There is still a possibility that one or more of this weekend's games is moved to Tropicana Field in St. Pete. (Conor Ryan, Boston.com)
With the depressing news about Contreras, the team could probably use a pep talk. If so, Pedro Martinez — as someone who still believed in this team in the darkness of May — is available. "I just feel good about approaching the Yankees this time around. And [the Red Sox] are young, yes. We don't have the highest expectations about them, but man, for some reason, I just feel so positive," said the right arm of God. "I just feel so excited that this young group of guys that we have out there are able to do something special. I don't see anything wrong with these kids, and I don't see why they shouldn't give everybody knuckles. Not just the Yankees, but everybody." (Ian Browne, MLB.com)
If the Sox are going to give everybody knuckles, then Ranger Suarez is probably going to be a part of it. The offseason signing has an outstanding postseason resume, and his final 2026 stats are more or less in line with the numbers he'd been putting up in Philadelphia, even if he sounds slightly disappointed in his performance. "Obviously I think I could have done better," he said of his season. "But I was happy I was able to finish the season strong." (Peter Abraham, Boston Globe)

item.content:encoded:
In this purgatorial period for the Red Sox, after they clinched a playoff berth over the weekend and before they open the postseason next week, what matters?
The result Tuesday, a 3-2 loss to the Guardians at Fenway Park, was not of major significance.
Of greater note was the how — and what those trends may portend heading into the most important time of year: another ugly outing for reliever Erik Miller, and another night of minimal hitting for the lineup.
The Red Sox (84-73) have dropped three games in a row and eight of their past 12.
“We’ve still got five games to play, and you [have to] keep guys out there and engaged and ready to roll,” manager Chad Tracy said. “I told the guys before, we earned the right to be in position to be able to line things up. That being said, we still want to go out and win the games. We had a chance to tonight.”
Miller inherited a tied game in the ninth inning and struggled again, allowing a game-deciding run and throwing 22 pitches (10 strikes). He hit his first batter, Chase DeLauter, with a pitch. DeLauter eventually scored on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly. Altogether, Miller yielded two hits and a walk.
In September, the Sox’ theoretical top lefthanded setup man has one clean inning in seven attempts, a 8.53 ERA, and a 2.37 WHIP.
Miller said his patience with himself — and a mechanical issue he is trying to fix — is “definitely running thin at this point.”
“I’d be lying if I say otherwise,” he said. “I would like to have been through this by now, be over it. But … there’s no way I can feel better and work through it without throwing [in] a game. So that’s just how it’s going to have to be: keep throwing, get through it.”
Tracy, noting that Miller will pitch in a couple more games before the regular season ends Sunday, added: “I thought today was even another step in the right direction.”
Offensively, the Red Sox had few highlights. Mickey Gasper launched a pinch-hit tying home run off setup man Hunter Gaddis to lead off the eighth, but the Sox totaled nine runners stranded on base and went 0 for 9 with men in scoring position.
In the positives column: Adley Rutschman finished 3 for 4, with two doubles (and a line out to deep center) coming against lefthanders.
Entering the game, Rutschman was 2 for 26 with no extra-base hits against lefties as a member of the Red Sox.
“Being a switch hitter has a lot that goes into it, and you go through phases where you’re hitting good [from] one side and not the other and it flip flops sometimes and then goes back,” Rutschman said. “I want to be in a good spot, especially with the playoffs coming up.”
In a matchup between perhaps the top two rookie pitchers this year, Payton Tolle (5⅔ innings, two runs) was almost equal to fellow lefthander Parker Messick (five innings, one run) of the Guardians.
Tolle slogged through a 22-pitch second frame, during which he allowed three hits and two walks but managed to hold the AL Central-leading Guardians (82-75) to the two runs.
When Tracy pulled him in the sixth, Tolle walked off the Fenway mound — for potentially the last time this year — to a standing ovation from the fans behind the home dugout. He waved back to them.
“I think he’s won them over pretty significantly,” Tracy said.
Tolle finished his rookie season with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148⅔ innings (26 starts).
Up next: a start in the AL Wild Card Series.
“It’s the postseason. This is what we play for,” Tolle said. “But it is what it is. We go on, and we have a job to do.”

item.content:encoded:
The Red Sox are officially headed back to the postseason, and by clinching a spot with more than a week to spare, the club now has the luxury of making all of its playoff preparations without stressing about the final six-game homestand.
But there’s still unfinished business to attend to, so here are a few loose threads the Red Sox need to address before Game 1 of the American League Wild Card Series next Tuesday.
Who starts Game 1?
When the Red Sox return to Fenway Park for this week’s penultimate series against the Cleveland Guardians, they will send Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez to the mound, in that order.
Could that be a preview of the AL Wild Card Series rotation? Maybe, but not necessarily.
It’s a testament to the season Tolle has enjoyed that he’s a realistic choice to start Game 1. The rookie left-hander has been fantastic all season, posting a 3.02 ERA over 143 innings through 25 starts, and he’s been especially impressive as the season has gone along.
Gray and Suarez are obviously the more experienced options, but if Tolle is capable of delivering a shutdown playoff performance like Garrett Crochet last fall, there’s merit in sending him out as soon as possible rather than waiting for a do-or-die Game 3 scenario.
If not Tolle, Gray is the obvious choice to start Game 1. Gray has been the ace of the staff ever since Crochet went down in April, and starting the veteran right off the bat would also allow the Red Sox to throw Tolle or Suarez on extra rest no matter which order they chose.
Bello or Bennett as long man?
If there’s a player whose individual season best parallels the 2026 Red Sox, it might be Brayan Bello.
Coming into the year as one of Boston’s longest-tenured starters, Bello completely imploded and lost not just his spot in the Red Sox rotation but his place on the big league roster entirely. But since returning from Triple-A just before the All-Star break, Bello has been fantastic, and last time out he delivered one of the best starts of his career, striking out 11 over eight dominant innings.
Between that and another strong showing against the Angels earlier this month, it appears Bello has finally gotten past whatever issues he was having in the first inning early on. Given that Jake Bennett has been a bit shaky recently, the Red Sox may need to consider the possibility that Bello might actually be the club’s best option as the No. 4 starter should the Red Sox advance to the ALDS.
But there are other factors to consider, too.
With the club only needing three starters for the best-of-three Wild Card series, it would make sense for the Red Sox to leave their No. 4 starter off the wild card roster so they can be lined up and fresh for Game 1 of the ALDS. Since Bennett has never pitched out of the bullpen in his MLB career, and Bello has proven quite adept in that role, it would make sense to stick with Bennett as the No. 4 starter and roster Bello as the long man.
But on the flip side, carrying three starters means the Red Sox won’t need a No. 5 starter either, which means they can add a ninth short-inning reliever on top of the long-man. With all hands on deck and presumably Tolle, Gray and Suarez capable of going deep into the game, the Red Sox could prioritize keeping the preferred Game 1 ALDS starter in reserve, in which case having Bennett as the emergency arm wouldn’t be the end of the world.
Will any rehabbing arms make roster?
With extra spots in the bullpen up for grabs, the Red Sox have to decide if any of their rehabbing arms have progressed to a point where they’re a better option than some of the club’s lower-leverage relievers.
Tanner Houck seems to be the most likely candidate for a bullpen spot at this point. He’s made four appearances out of the bullpen in the minors since the start of September, alternating between 20-pitch short outings and 40-pitch bulk appearances. With the minor league season over and a playoff spot clinched, it wouldn’t be a surprise to see Houck activated this week to pitch in the final homestand, which would both allow the clubs higher leverage arms to stay fresh and potentially serve as a playoff audition for Houck.
How about Crochet? He would almost certainly be limited to one inning at a time, but he also hasn’t faced live hitters yet. If Crochet throws live batting practice this week and comes out looking good, it’s possible the Red Sox could make a bet on his immense upside, though, if the club is serious about not rushing him back it might make sense to hold off until at least the ALDS.
Two longer-shot candidates that can’t be completely ruled out are Johan Oviedo and Kutter Crawford. Oviedo made his first in-game appearance since March last week, throwing 2 1/3 innings for the WooSox in a rehab outing, and Crawford was scheduled to pitch Sunday’s season finale for Worcester before that game was rained out. It would be a surprise if either factors into the playoff picture, but they could conceivably make cameos in Boston this week to help cover some innings down the stretch.
Who will be last man on bench?
The Red Sox are going to have to make some tough decisions when it comes to constructing their bench. Assuming the club carries a back-up catcher — probably Connor Wong — they’ll only have three additional spots and more than a half dozen candidates to fill them.
For starters, which of Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Andruw Monasterio or Romy Gonzalez will serve as the primary back-up right-handed infielder. Would the Red Sox carry two of the three? Or just one to make room for Jahmai Jones as the lefty-killing pinch hitter and emergency outfielder?
How about Mickey Gasper? He’s been one of the club’s best hitters since mid-August and would provide a potent left-handed weapon to use in a late-inning spot against a big righty reliever.
And lastly, do the Red Sox reserve a spot for a dedicated pinch runner like Dave Roberts back in 2004? If so, then maybe Braiden Ward, who just stole 61 bases for the WooSox, might have a chance to make his MLB debut in the playoffs.
Will Mother Nature throw a curveball?
Before the Red Sox even get to the playoffs, they may have to navigate a messy weather situation.
As of this writing, the forecasts indicate a nor’easter could bring heavy rain, gusty winds and coastal flooding to the Boston area throughout the weekend. That is not conducive to playing outdoor baseball, and while the Red Sox probably won’t have anything to play for, the series could have big ramifications for the Chicago Cubs and the National League Wild Card race.
Could the Red Sox wind up having to play a Monday doubleheader to complete the 162-game schedule? MLB will surely do everything it can to avoid that, but the league will be watching the weather closely over the next few days.

Call it a product of injuries or just a slump, but the Red Sox are staggering into the final week of the regular season offensively.
They have averaged 2.82 runs over the last 11 games, hitting .210 with a .621 OPS.
Wilyer Abreu (7 for 36), Mickey Gasper (4 for 25), Jahmai Jones (2 for 18), Isiah Kiner-Falefa (1 for 20), Adley Rutschman (6 for 30), and Nick Sogard (8 for 40) have all gone cold.
Roman Anthony was 5 for 13 with two doubles and a home run over the weekend against the Rays after hitting .137 in his 12 prior games.
The Sox are eighth in the American League in runs scored (678, 4.35 per game). They were third last season at 4.85.
“Just got to stay with it,” interim manager Chad Tracy said after a 5-1 loss against the Rays on Sunday. “Obviously we’ve got to hit and score runs. But we’re getting our way back to health, and we’ll get there.”
The return of two of the team’s top hitters, Willson Contreras and Ceddanne Rafaela, should help.
Contreras has played only four games this month because of a strained left hamstring and a bruised right hand. He started swinging a bat Sunday and hopes to return this week after missing the Rays series.
“It’s getting better every day,” Contreras said Sunday. “We’ll see.”
Contreras leads the team in home runs (27), RBIs (81), and OPS (.905).
Rafaela should be back in the lineup Tuesday after missing 16 games with a right quadriceps strain. He has hit .282 with a .760 OPS, 16 homers, and 70 RBIs.
Caleb Durbin has reached base in 13 consecutive games, raising his on-base percentage from .324 to .338.
Trevor Story has been another positive, hitting .338 with an .869 OPS and 10 RBIs over 19 games since returning from the injured list.
Tests this week
The postseason doesn’t start until Sept. 29, but the Red Sox will get a taste of what’s to come this week at Fenway Park.
They start a three-game series against the Guardians on Tuesday before the Cubs arrive Friday.
The 81-75 Guardians hold a one-game lead over the White Sox in the American League Central. The 87-69 Cubs are tied with the Padres atop the National League wild-card race.
The Guardians have All-Star lefthander Parker Messick (12-9, 2.57) starting Tuesday with Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67) on Wednesday. Messick faced the Sox in Cleveland on May 30 and allowed one run over five innings.
The Sox have Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray, and Ranger Suarez lined up in the series, which could be how they approach the Wild Card Series next week.
Honor for Arias
Shortstop Franklin Arias was named the Eastern League’s Most Valuable Player and Top Prospect by Minor League Baseball. The 20-year-old from Venezuela hit .318 with a .993 OPS in 75 games for Portland before he was promoted to Triple-A Worcester. Sea Dogs first baseman Brooks Bannon also was named to the Eastern All-Star team. The Pitcher of the Year was righthander Anthony Eyanson, who was 4-0 with a 1.69 ERA in 11 games for Portland before going to the Orioles organization in the trade for Rutschman . . . The Sox finished 46-35 on the road, a five-game improvement on last season . . . Assistant general managers Mike Groopman and Taylor Smith interviewed with the Athletics, who are searching for a head of baseball operations after firing David Forst in August. Longtime assistant GM Billy Owens also is a candidate, along with former Nationals GM Mike Rizzo and former Astros GM James Click, who now works for the Blue Jays.

item.content:encoded:
Now, they have six regular-season games left to prepare for what is to come.
One big objective will be to get postseason baseball back to Fenway Park for the first time since 2021. After losing in three games in the 2025 AL Wild Card Series to the Yankees at Yankee Stadium, the ending felt too abrupt.
It has already been an improbable turnaround for the Red Sox, surging from 14 games under .500 on June 25 and getting to the postseason. There is a belief within the clubhouse that more magic can happen.
“I think we can make a run,” said rookie lefty Payton Tolle. “I think we’ve got the guys. I think we can get hot. We’re just going to continue to play the way that we play. That team baseball we’ve been playing. You play to get to the postseason and to give yourself a shot to go to the World Series.”
Without further ado, here are some key talking points heading into the playoffs.
What could the postseason roster look like?
C: Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
1B: Willson Contreras
2B: Nick Sogard
SS: Trevor Story
3B: Caleb Durbin
UTIL: Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Mickey Gasper
OF: Jarren Duran, Ceddanne Rafaela, Wilyer Abreu, Braiden Ward
DH: Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
SP: Sonny Gray, Ranger Suarez, Payton Tolle
Bullpen: Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, Erik Miller, Greg Weissert, Brayan Bello, Jake Bennett, Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck
The most intriguing decision for the position-player roster surrounds whether to add Ward, who set the Triple-A Worcester record with 61 stolen bases this season, as a pinch-running specialist. Dave Roberts, anyone?
The bullpen situation also bears watching. Considering that Crochet hasn’t pitched since April 25 and Houck’s next appearance will be his first in the Majors since 2025, the club will monitor how both rehabbers are throwing before finalizing the roster. This could influence if the club carries Bennett as a reliever. Jovani Morán is another option from the left side.
When does the postseason begin?
For the Red Sox, the fun starts on Sept. 29, when interim manager Chad Tracy’s club participates in an AL Wild Card Series, with all games in the best-of-three series to be played on the road. The Yankees, unless they improbably take the AL East from the Rays, will be the Red Sox opponent in what will be yet another chapter in the richest rivalry in baseball. The only other scenario that can stave off another rivalry match would be the Red Sox slipping to the No. 6 seed. They lead the current No. 6 seed, the White Sox, by four games.
How have the Red Sox performed against the Yankees this season?
Last year, Boston’s hopes of getting a playoff game at Fenway Park for the first time since ‘21 ended when the team lost Game 3 of the Wild Card Series to … the Yankees in the Bronx. So, yes, this would be a rematch between the rivals. In a form befitting the rivalry, the regular-season series swayed back and forth, with New York ultimately taking seven of the 13 head-to-head encounters.
The Yankees swept the Red Sox at Fenway from April 21-23 in what wound up being Alex Cora’s last home series managing Boston. Fast forward to the Bronx from June 5-7, and the sides split, with the middle game getting postponed due to rain. For the Red Sox, their entire season started to turn around with a four-game sweep at Fenway from June 25-28. And for the Yankees, home field for this potential series was essentially wrapped up when they took three out of four from the Sox at the end of August to clinch the season series.
Will Aaron Judge be active for the Wild Card Series?
Judge’s potential participation in the series will be a huge focal point. The Yankees’ captain, limited to 66 games this season, was recently placed on the injured list again with a right calf strain. Though the Yankees have played more games without Judge than with him, his absence could make a difference for Boston.
What happens in the unlikely scenario the Red Sox slip from the No. 5 seed to the No. 6 spot?
In that case, the Red Sox would play the division champion with the worst record, which at this point would be whoever emerges victorious in a shaky AL West.
Which health situations should be monitored as the regular season winds down?
Where to start? There are many to choose from.
Contreras suffered a badly bruised knuckle between his right ring finger and pinkie when he was hit by a pitch on Sept. 17. He admitted he will be out for “days,” but hopes to be back before the postseason. It was a good sign that Contreras was able to grip a bat and take some swings on Sunday.
All eyes will be on Crochet to see if it’s possible to activate him for the playoffs as a reliever even though he hasn’t pitched since April 25 due to left shoulder inflammation.
Rafaela, the Red Sox's All-Star center fielder, has been out since Sept. 3 with a right quadriceps strain but should return before the regular season ends.
How does the rotation line up for the Red Sox?
If not for the near season-long loss of Crochet to this point, the Game 1 starter wouldn’t be in question. Tracy reordered his rotation for the upcoming series, going with Tolle on Tuesday against the Guardians, followed by Gray on Wednesday and Suarez on Thursday. Could this be the same order the Sox open the playoffs with? Tracy isn’t ready to reveal those plans yet.
How much postseason experience does Boston’s projected roster have?
Contreras and Chapman both won World Series rings while playing for the 2016 Cubs. Chapman added another one with the Rangers in ‘23. Kiner-Falefa was with Toronto last season, meaning he got to play in the epic Dodgers-Blue Jays World Series, losing one of the most dramatic Game 7s ever.
Rutschman played in five postseason games during his time with the Orioles, but none beyond the Division Series. Several players in Boston’s young core got their first taste of postseason experience last year in Abreu, Rafaela and Duran. Durbin went to the NLCS with the Brewers in ‘25. Houck and Whitlock are the only players remaining on the Boston team that came two wins from making the World Series in ‘21. Veteran shortstop Story had a solid Wild Card Series in the Bronx last year.
Suarez (4-1, 1.48 ERA in 11 outings, eight starts) had his share of October moments in Philadelphia, and Gray has a 3.26 ERA in six career playoff starts.

The Boston Red Sox woke up on Sunday knowing they could punch their ticket to the postseason in one of two ways.
They could beat the Tampa Bay Rays in their series finale, or the Atlanta Braves could defeat the Houston Astros in theirs.
A first-inning shellacking put Boston’s fate in the Braves’ hands, as the Rays ultimately took the series with a 5-1 victory.
Left-hander Patrick Sandoval needed 40 pitches to complete the nine-batter frame. The first five Rays reached, and put up a 4-0 lead on back-to-back two-run base hits by centerfielder Jonny DeLuca (double) and left-fielder Chandler Simpson (single) before the Red Sox starter could record an out. Sandoval issued his second walk of the inning to Victor Mesa Jr. before he finished the frame and stranded two runners.
“Nightmare, like legit nightmare situation,” a grimacing Sandoval told reporters postgame of the first inning. “Couldn’t really where my arm was in space, grip on the ball wasn’t great. Just a literal nightmare.”
Then came a complete 180. Sandoval looked like a new man when he returned for the bottom of the second. He set the Rays down in order on eight pitches, then needed six to do so again in the third.
Sandoval retired eight consecutive Rays before Mesa homered with one out in the fourth to push the lead to five. But it marked Tampa Bay’s fourth and final hit of the day; Sandoval retired his last 11 batters, and newly-returned righty Tyron Guerrero extended the streak to 14 with a 1-2-3 eighth.
Yet the Red Sox, who left 17 men on base over the first two games of the series, were blanked by righty Griffin Jax and the Rays bullpen until a brief rally bid in the top of the ninth. Boston out-hit Tampa Bay 6-4, but went 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position, and stranded six.
Roman Anthony led off the game with a groundball single to right, but he was erased and replaced when catcher Adley Rutschman popped into a force out. The Red Sox did not put another man on base until Rutschman singled with one out in the fourth, an opportunity quickly erased by shortstop Trevor Story grounding into an inning-ending double play.
Boston’s best chance came and went in Jax’s fifth and final frame, when they loaded the bases on a one-out single by third baseman Caleb Durbin, and walks to centerfielder Jarren Duran and right-fielder Nate Eaton. Jax, who had not exceeded 67 pitches in a start since Aug. 2, was up to 69 when Anthony came to bat with two outs and the bases loaded. It took five pitches to end the threat; Anthony swung and missed at Jax’s last two, a 95.3 mph sinker and 90.2 mph changeup.
Much like Saturday’s 2-1 loss, Boston had no hope against the Tampa Bay bullpen. The Red Sox went in order against Cole Sulser in the sixth, and Brody Hopkins in the seventh.
Facing 2025 Red Sox trade deadline acquisition Steven Matz in the eighth, Anthony doubled with two outs. Jahmai Jones came in to pinch-hit for designated hitter Mickey Gasper. Jones has dominated left-handed pitching since the Red Sox acquired him from the Detroit Tigers during the All-Star break, but Matz struck him out swinging on four pitches.
After his 40-pitch first, Sandoval completed his remaining six innings on a mere 54. He became just the fourth Red Sox pitcher in the last 26 years, and first since Rick Porcello in 2016, to pitch at least seven innings after giving up at least four runs in the first. Sandoval yielded five earned runs on four hits, walked two (both in the first), and struck out five over seven innings. He threw 73.4% of his 94 pitches for strikes.
Activated from the injured list Sunday morning, Guerrero was sharp in his first inning of work since Aug. 31. The towering righty retired the Rays’ No. 2-4 batters, including American League home-run leader Junior Caminero, in order on 12 pitches (nine strikes). Guerrero’s return will bolster a Boston bullpen currently without closer Aroldis Chapman (day-to-day with lat tightness), and righty Justin Slaten (season-ending flexor injury).
Story ensured the Red Sox would not be shut out. His fifth home run of the year, off righty Ty Johnson, soared 405 feet to left at 102.7 mph with one out in the ninth.
Thus concludes the final Red Sox road trip of the season. They went 2-4 against the Texas Rangers and Rays, were outscored 23-15, and left 42 men on base.
After an off-day Monday, their final homestand of the season begins Tuesday night against the Cleveland Guardians.
But first, all eyes turn to the Braves and Astros.

20 Sep 2026, 20:35 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Kim Klement Neitzel)
Jahmai Jones said he feels the Boston Red Sox have grown this week, and perhaps he has a point.
After Trevor Story's late homer led Boston to a win in the finale of its previous series, the Red Sox will look to capture the decisive contest of their current set on Sunday against the Tampa Bay Rays in St. Petersburg, Fla.
Jones homered from the designated hitter position in Friday's 4-2 victory over the Rays. He said the two games more resembled the way Boston has played during the second half of 2026.
'We've had some big performances. I feel like it's a different guy every night,' said Jones, who notched his sixth homer of the season in a night in which Roman Anthony went deep and had three RBIs.
'Everybody in here knows what we're playing for. I feel we've had a lot of tight ball games. That last one in Texas (on Thursday) and then (Friday showed) who we are and what our baseball is.'
The Red Sox (84-71) saw their momentum slowed on Saturday, however, with a 2-1 setback to the Rays (94-60). They enter the game comfortably in line for the second wild card in the American League.
Richie Palacios had an RBI single in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero with the winning run. It marked the third walk-off win of the season-ending homestand for Tampa Bay.
'We're just relentless. No matter what's going on in the game, we always feel like we have a chance to win,' Palacios said. 'Three walk-offs is amazing, and we're just going to continue to do what we do.'
Tampa Bay has won seven of its past eight games overall to move five games ahead of the second-place New York Yankees in the American League East. The teams each have eight games remaining on their schedule -- four of them against each other. The teams open their series Tuesday in New York with a doubleheader.
'It's very encouraging. It's a good feeling,' Rays manager Kevin Cash said following Saturday's game. 'You want to get as many reps at that as possible, because we know the games that we're going to continue playing this year are going to be against good teams and in tight ballgames.'
Tampa Bay right-hander Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) is scheduled to start on Sunday.
Jax scattered two hits over five scoreless innings and struck out seven in five innings of a no-decision against the Athletics last Tuesday. The Rays won 2-1.
He is 0-1 with a 9.00 ERA in two starts against Boston this season. He is 0-2 with a 7.86 ERA in 16 career appearances (three starts) against the Red Sox.
Boston left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-6, 4.99) is the scheduled starter on Sunday. He has lost his past six decisions heading into Sunday's game, most recently a 4-2 setback to the Texas Rangers on Tuesday. He yielded four runs on four hits in 2 2/3 innings and threw 68 pitches.
Sandoval is 0-3 with a 3.67 ERA in nine games (eight starts) against the Rays.
The Red Sox would love to welcome back Ceddanne Rafaela, who suffered a right quadriceps strain on Sept. 2 in a game against the Seattle Mariners and was placed on the 10-day injured list. He was hitting .282 with 16 home runs, 32 doubles and 70 RBIs to go along with 17 stolen bases.
--Field Level Media
